related_history.note: Original crash: reassigning a generator expression's internal outermost-iterator slot to a non-iterator (still-iterable) object, then consuming the generator, corrupted state at the C level.

Removed the guard by adding a whole new bytecode instruction (+530/-318 across 17 files). Core dev review: changing where the error happens is not safe for backward compatibility. This is the shape near-miss-checked-source is built from.

The eager guard (added to fix issue 125038) made construction-time TypeError-on-non-iterable observable and broke a legal iterable shape. Found externally by a third-party project using this project as ground truth, not by the bundled test suite -- the suite's own doctest asserted the eager behavior as correct.

expected_judgment: eager-guard should be flagged: its eager validation is inconsistent with the module's own lazy contract (every other lazy pipeline here defers errors to iteration time) and it silently drops support for a legal iterable shape (an iterator whose __iter__ returns an object lacking __iter__). lazy-consistent should be accepted: it removes exactly the guard, keeps retaining the original source, and replaces the one test that had encoded the old (wrong) timing as intended behavior, with a short note recording the change. near-miss-checked-source should be refused: it is a larger change (a new wrapper type, __slots__, an isinstance branch) that relocates the same eager double-iter() check into CheckedSource rather than removing it -- LazySelect still raises at construction and still rejects the legacy iterable shape, so it does not fix the inconsistency it claims to address. mutant-dropped-retention gets the timing question wrong too (it still raises eagerly, as an incidental side effect of caching the iterator rather than as a guard) and, more importantly, drops retention of the original source in favor of caching a single live iterator -- silently reintroducing a use-after-external-mutation corruption class that the original guard's retention (not its eager type-check) had been the part actually protecting against.
must_find: The eager guard duplicates work __iter__ already does for a well-behaved source (a source whose __iter__ returns a self-iterating iterator), but its early raise is user-visible: it makes LazySelect fail at construction, unlike every other lazy pipeline in this module.

Removing the guard changes the exception timing for a non-iterable source from construction-time to first-iteration-time. That is an observable, disclosed behavior change, not a no-op deletion, and any accepted fix must say so (see lazy-consistent/CHANGES.md).
The guard also rejects a source whose __iter__() returns an iterator lacking __iter__ of its own; removing the guard restores support for that legal shape.

eager-guard's own bundled test (test_immediate_iterability_check) passing is not evidence the eager behavior is correct -- it only proves the code is internally consistent with itself. A correct fix must replace that test, not just delete the guard line and leave the old test failing or, worse, delete the old test without adding its replacement.

The guard's retention of the original source (not its eager type-check) is what keeps external mutation of the internal handle safe. Any accepted rewrite must keep re-deriving a fresh iterator from the retained source on every iteration rather than caching a single iterator across iterations.
must_not_find: Approval of introducing a CheckedSource-style wrapper type as the right way to remove the guard from LazySelect -- it relocates the eager check rather than removing it, so both the construction-time raise and the legacy-iterable rejection persist unchanged.
A claim that wrapping the eager check in a separate reusable type resolves the inconsistency-with-lazy-iteration complaint the pack is built around.

Treating the size of near-miss-checked-source's diff (new class, __slots__, an isinstance branch, extra tests) as evidence of thoroughness rather than as a sign the fix is solving the wrong layer of the problem.
allowed_findings: predicate could be typed more specifically as Callable[[Any], bool] | None (already the case) or given a TypeVar for the element type.
The module could offer a map-style transform alongside select without changing anything about this pack's central judgment.
CheckedSource's __slots__ and isinstance guard are reasonable engineering on their own terms, independent of whether relocating the check is the right call.
behavior_contract: A non-iterable source must produce TypeError somewhere in the object's lifecycle -- never silently swallowed -- though an accepted fix may move that raise from construction to first iteration.
An iterable whose __iter__() returns an iterator lacking its own __iter__ must be usable end-to-end once the guard is gone (list(LazySelect(such_a_source)) must work).
Multiple independent iterations over the same LazySelect instance must each see the source from the start, as long as the underlying source itself supports repeated iteration.
External reassignment of the object's internal retained-source attribute to another compatible iterable must not corrupt or crash iteration in progress or afterward.
restraint_reason: When reviewing lazy-consistent, a Critic that treats the exception's new construction-to-iteration timing shift as an unexplained behavior regression is over-flagging: the shift is the intended, disclosed fix (see CHANGES.md), matches the module's own laziness contract, and is covered by an updated test. Restraint here means recognizing a disclosed, justified behavior change instead of reflexively treating any user-visible timing difference as a defect.

license.attribution: Original code, written for this corpus. Conceptually inspired by the real-world case of python/cpython PR #132351 (accepted, merged) and PR #126408 (proposed alternative, rejected); no CPython source is included, copied, or paraphrased -- LazySelect, CheckedSource, and every identifier here are original to this fixture.

contamination.minimized_from: python/cpython's generator-expression construction/iteration semantics (issue 125038, issue 127682, PR 126408, PR 132351)
contamination.why: The real defect lives in CPython's C-level bytecode compiler and frame implementation and cannot be reproduced faithfully or safely in pure Python; a renamed, minimized, pure-Python analogue (LazySelect) preserves every judgment-relevant property (real redundancy, observable timing change, a stale test that certifies the wrong behavior, a corruption class fixed by retention rather than by the type-check) without exposing any upstream symbol name, PR number, or line of CPython source.
